key_insight: Pretrained language models implicitly encode grammaticality in their internal representations even when token probabilities do not sharply separate grammatical from ungrammatical strings; a simple probe can extract this latent grammaticality signal across diverse constructions.
problem_solved: Bridges the gap between probability-based evaluation and human notions of grammatical well-formedness by showing where and how grammatical judgments are represented inside LMs, enabling reliable discrimination of grammatical vs. ungrammatical sentences beyond surface string likelihoods.
method: Collect minimal-pair and broader sentence sets with grammatical vs. ungrammatical labels across syntactic phenomena.
Extract hidden states (layer-wise) from pretrained LMs and train lightweight probes (e.g., linear classifiers) to predict grammaticality from representations.
Analyze probe accuracy, generalization across constructions, and representational geometry (layer and head effects) to localize grammaticality signals.
impact: Provides practitioners a practical way to read out grammatical knowledge from models without changing model training; useful for evaluation, targeted debugging, and building grammar-aware controls for generation and filtering.
visual_elements: t-SNE/UMAP plot of hidden-state embeddings colored by grammatical vs. ungrammatical to show clustering of grammaticality.
Layer-wise bar chart showing probe accuracy by model layer to identify where grammaticality is most explicit.
ROC/precision-recall curves comparing probability-based ranking vs. probe-based grammaticality classification.
Schematic: minimal-pair example -> LM hidden states -> linear probe -> grammaticality label (simple pipeline diagram).
paper_title: Implicit Representations of Grammaticality in Language Models
paper_authors: Yingshan Susan Wang, Linlu Qiu, Zhaofeng Wu, Roger P. Levy, Yoon Kim
